prize_parts.citation: for introducing firm heterogeneity and selection into trade theory and for showing how reallocation across firms shapes the gains from trade

statement.case_for: Firm heterogeneity and selection moved international trade from sector-level to firm-level analysis. The Melitz (2003) model and the Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple extension to exporting versus FDI identify a mechanism, reallocation toward more productive firms, that was absent from the representative-firm and new-trade-theory frameworks. The mechanism generated sharp, testable predictions (exporter premia, selection into export markets, within-industry reallocation after liberalisation). These have been checked against firm-level data in many countries over two decades. The idea has also spread beyond trade into macro, growth and development, where reallocation and misallocation are now standard organising concepts. This matters for my own reading of firm dynamics and growth. Helpman's earlier work on differentiated-product trade adds a second, separable layer of credit. After reconsidering my opening, I put B048 first because its attribution and empirical standing are cleaner than those of my previous first choice, B001. The Krugman prize in 2008 covered earlier new trade theory, and this is a distinct advance on it.
statement.case_against: Credit is not fully captured by the ballot names. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum developed closely related firm-level facts and models, and they are not on this entry, so a Melitz-Helpman prize could be read as under-crediting the empirical foundations. Redding's quantitative and spatial work, which I included in my opening, is left out here as a later strand. The size of the welfare gains from selection also depends on functional-form choices such as the Pareto productivity assumption, as the quantitative trade debate shows. Trade has also had a prize in 2008, which could affect field balance, though not merit.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B048 first for its testable predictions and durable empirical record. She ranks B001 only seventh because the legal-origins thesis is weaker on measurement, coding and causal identification than its influence suggests.
responses.response: I agree with her on B048 and have partly updated toward her on B001. In my opening I weighted B001's influence heavily. The causal and measurement critiques she lists (coding of the anti-director index, endogeneity of legal origin) are serious, and the field itself has moved away from the strongest form of the hypothesis. I still think B001 created a large research programme, which is why I keep it as an alternative. Under common criteria, though, B048's core predictions have held up better under replication than B001's causal claims. I do not share her view that Redding is difficult to separate in B048. I now agree he is a later strand, but for the opposite reason: his work builds on the framework rather than defining it.

responses.point: Strömberg ranks B001 first. He credits an exceptional reach across corporate finance, comparative law and development, while acknowledging the measurement criticism and the cost of excluding Vishny.
responses.response: I share his view of the reach and I ranked B001 first in my opening for that reason. Reach across fields is not the same as a well-identified discovery, however. He himself lists the Doing Business and anti-director index critiques and the unresolved question of whether legal origin is causal or a proxy for history. A prize citation would have to say what was established, and for B001 that is the contested part. The three-name cap also forces out Vishny, who co-authored the core papers. For B048 the cap costs less, because the two credited names carry the central model and its main extension. I would not rule B001 out, but I do not think it should lead.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B015 first. He values the combination of credible designs and conceptual framing in the task-based and China-shock work, and notes the tension in what three names can cover across the technology and trade strands.
responses.response: I rank B015 highly too (second in my opening) and agree that its policy relevance is exceptional. My reservation is attribution and overlap. The task framework builds on work by Acemoglu, Levy and Murnane, and Acemoglu was recognised in 2024, with Goldin in 2023 on related labour themes. A three-name cap also forces a choice between Katz's skill-demand strand and Dorn's role in the China-shock papers. The size and persistence of the China-shock effects are still debated. I think B015 is a strong candidate, but its credit structure is less settled than that of B048, so I keep it as an alternative rather than the lead.

responses.point: Enflo also ranks B048 first and treats the Melitz-Helpman pairing as the cleanest credit. She sees Redding's quantitative and spatial work as a separate, later strand and flags Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum and Yeaple as outside the ballot entry.
responses.response: I accept her argument for the narrower credit. In my opening I added Redding, but the discovery itself, selection of heterogeneous firms into exporting and the resulting reallocation gains, is carried by Melitz and Helpman. I therefore drop Redding. I share her concern about the people outside the ballot, which is why I list it as an unresolved issue instead of treating the two-name credit as free of cost.

uncertainties: Whether the committee would want the empirical firm-level foundations (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) recognised, which this ballot entry cannot accommodate.
How much of Helpman's credit is better placed on the trade-politics and growth entry, since he appears on more than one ballot.
How sensitive the welfare-gain results are to functional-form assumptions, and whether this affects the claim to a robust discovery.

Whether B001 should rank above B048 if the legal-origins critiques are judged less damaging than I currently do. I rely on my own knowledge of the literature and have not independently verified the sources.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent for the preferred B048 part or the alternatives B001 and B015. The supplied profile does disclose a long-running collaboration with Peter Klenow (a credited name on B007, which is not in my configuration), and close colleagues at IIES, namely the chair and the secretary. These are disclosed, not adjudicated.
